# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for those looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution, with the core use case being team collaboration and communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to own and control their data, whereas Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is relatively easy to set up.
* Scalability: Slack is more scalable and can handle large teams, while Element's scalability depends on the server infrastructure.
* Feature difference: Element has end-to-end encryption, while Slack only offers encryption in transit.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Slack:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Scalable and reliable
* Wide range of integrations
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data
**Element:**
* Self-hosted and open-source
* End-to-end encryption
* Customizable and extensible
* Free and cost-effective
* Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for large teams that require a scalable and reliable communication platform, and are willing to pay for it. It's also a good option for teams that don't have the technical expertise to set up and maintain a self-hosted solution. Element, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams that value control over their data and want a cost-effective solution. It's also a good option for teams with technical expertise that can set up and maintain a self-hosted solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data in JSON format using the Slack API.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it to your needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data.
4. Configure your Element instance to connect to your existing authentication system.
5. Test your Element instance to ensure everything is working as expected.

---

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element's scalability depends on the server infrastructure, which can be a challenge for large teams. However, for teams that value control over their data and want a cost-effective solution, Element is a good choice, and we recommend switching from Slack to Element if you have a small to medium-sized team and don't require a lot of integrations.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't require a lot of integrations
* Teams with technical expertise that can set up and maintain a self-hosted solution
* Organizations that value control over their data and want a cost-effective solution
* Teams that don't require a lot of customer support
* Teams with less than 50 users that want to save on costs

## FAQ
### Is Element free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted. However, you will need to pay for the server infrastructure to host it.
### Can I use Element with a large team?
Yes, but Element's scalability depends on the server infrastructure, which can be a challenge for large teams.
### Is Element secure?
Yes, Element has end-to-end encryption and is considered secure.
### Can I integrate Element with other tools?
Yes, Element has a range of integrations available, but not as many as Slack.
### Is Element easy to set up?
No, Element requires technical expertise to set up and maintain.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for teams, offering real-time messaging, file sharing, and integrations with third-party services. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, potentially driven by the desire for greater control over their data or to reduce costs. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is often related to data ownership, cost, or specific feature requirements.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Slack charges per user, while Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option.
* Data Ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their data on their own servers, whereas Slack stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup Complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms can scale to meet the needs of large teams, but Mattermost's self-hosted option provides more flexibility in this regard.
* Integration with GitHub: Mattermost has native integration with GitHub, allowing for seamless issue tracking and project management, whereas Slack relies on third-party integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party services
* Robust mobile apps
* Strong support for audio and video conferencing
* Limited control over data storage and security
### Mattermost
* Self-hosted option for greater control over data
* Customizable and extensible through plugins and APIs
* Strong focus on security and compliance
* Native integration with GitHub
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations with third-party services. It's suitable for small to medium-sized teams that don't require a high degree of customization or control over their data. On the other hand, Mattermost is ideal for larger teams or organizations that require a high degree of control over their data and security. It's also a good fit for teams that are already familiar with self-hosted solutions and have the technical expertise to manage their own servers.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either on your own hardware or through a cloud provider.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to import your Slack data, which should be in JSON format.
4. Configure your Mattermost server to match your team's needs, including setting up users, channels, and integrations.
5. Test your Mattermost setup to ensure that everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready platform for teams that require a high degree of control over their data and security. However, it may not be the best choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations with third-party services. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's self-hosted option requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and manage. We recommend Mattermost for teams that are already familiar with self-hosted solutions and have the technical expertise to manage their own servers. Teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations may want to stick with Slack.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't require a wide range of integrations and want to reduce costs.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that require a high degree of control over their data and security.
* Large teams (more than 50 users) that are already familiar with self-hosted solutions and have the technical expertise to manage their own servers.
* Teams that don't require audio and video conferencing features.
* Teams that prioritize security and compliance above all else.

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Slack?
No, Slack does not offer a self-hosted option.
### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost is free to use, but you'll need to pay for your own server costs if you choose to self-host.
### Can I integrate Mattermost with GitHub?
Yes, Mattermost has native integration with GitHub.
### Is Mattermost as easy to use as Slack?
No, Mattermost has a steeper learning curve due to its self-hosting requirements.
### Can I export my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, you can export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool and then import it into Mattermost.

# Notion vs AppFlowy (2026)

## Overview
Notion and AppFlowy are two popular tools used for note-taking, project management, and team collaboration. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from Notion to AppFlowy, particularly those seeking a self-hosted solution with more control over their data. The core use case for both tools is to provide a flexible and customizable workspace for teams to organize their work and collaborate effectively.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Notion charges $8-$20 per user per month, while AppFlowy is free.
* Data ownership: AppFlowy allows users to self-host their data, giving them full control and ownership, whereas Notion stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: AppFlowy requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting, compared to Notion's straightforward sign-up process.
* Scalability: Notion is designed to handle large teams and enterprises, while AppFlowy's scalability is still being developed and tested.
* Integration difference: Notion has a wider range of integrations with third-party apps, including Google Drive and Trello, whereas AppFlowy's integration list is currently more limited.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Notion | AppFlowy |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $8-$20/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $400-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1600-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Notion:**
* Pros:
	+ Easy to use and set up
	+ Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
	+ Scalable for large teams and enterprises
	+ Robust customer support
	+ Regular updates with new features
* Cons:
	+ Expensive for large teams
	+ Limited control over data ownership
	+ Proprietary license
**AppFlowy:**
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Self-hosting option for full data control
	+ Customizable and flexible workspace
	+ Community-driven development
	+ GPL 3.0 license
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve
	+ Limited integrations with third-party apps
	+ Still developing and testing scalability
	+ Requires technical expertise for self-hosting
	+ Limited customer support

## When to Choose Each
Notion is suitable for teams of all sizes that require a straightforward, easy-to-use collaboration tool with a wide range of integrations and robust customer support. It's ideal for teams that don't mind paying a premium for a proprietary solution and are willing to compromise on data ownership. On the other hand, AppFlowy is perfect for small to medium-sized teams, startups, or individuals who value data ownership, customization, and flexibility. It's also a great choice for teams with technical expertise who can self-host and manage their own instance.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Notion data in Markdown format using the Notion export tool.
2. Set up an AppFlowy instance, either self-hosted or using a cloud provider.
3. Use the AppFlowy import tool to import your Notion data in Markdown format.
4. Configure your AppFlowy workspace to match your Notion setup, including pages, blocks, and templates.
5. Test and refine your AppFlowy setup to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
AppFlowy is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks certain features and polish compared to Notion. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that AppFlowy's scalability is still being developed and tested, which may impact large teams or enterprises. However, for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who value data ownership and customization, AppFlowy is a great choice, and we recommend switching from Notion to take advantage of its free and open-source nature.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need advanced integrations
* Startups who value data ownership and customization
* Individuals who want a free and open-source note-taking solution
* Teams who require self-hosting for security or compliance reasons
* Developers who want a customizable and flexible workspace

## FAQ
### Is AppFlowy free?
Yes, AppFlowy is completely free and open-source. It's licensed under the GPL 3.0, which means you can use, modify, and distribute it without any costs.
### Can I self-host AppFlowy?
Yes, AppFlowy allows self-hosting, giving you full control over your data and instance. You can host it on your own server or use a cloud provider.
### Is AppFlowy compatible with Notion?
AppFlowy can import Notion data in Markdown format, making it easy to migrate from Notion. However, some features and formatting may not be compatible.
### Does AppFlowy have a mobile app?
Not yet, but the AppFlowy team is working on developing a mobile app for iOS and Android devices.
### Can I use AppFlowy for large teams?
AppFlowy is still developing and testing its scalability, so it's not recommended for large teams or enterprises at this time.

title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Obsidian is a free, self-hosted alternative to Notion. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Logseq free to use?
Yes. Logseq is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Logseq?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Logseq import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Logseq get regular updates?
Yes. Logseq has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Logseq without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

# GitHub vs GitLab

## Overview

GitHub is the world largest code hosting platform, owned by Microsoft, with 100 million developers. GitLab is a complete DevOps platform that can be fully self-hosted, offering everything from Git hosting to CI/CD and container registries.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub free tier is generous; GitLab Community Edition is fully free to self-host
- **CI/CD**: GitLab has more powerful built-in CI/CD pipelines; GitHub Actions is catching up
- **Self-hosting**: GitLab is designed to be self-hosted; GitHub Enterprise self-hosted is expensive
- **Feature scope**: GitLab is a complete DevSecOps platform; GitHub focuses on developer collaboration
- **Community**: GitHub has a dramatically larger open-source community and project discoverability

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### GitLab

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [gitlabhq/gitlabhq](https://github.com/gitlabhq/gitlabhq) * ~24k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub suits open-source projects wanting maximum community visibility or teams deeply integrated with GitHub Actions workflows.

**Choose GitLab if:** GitLab self-hosted is ideal for enterprises needing full control over their DevOps stack or regulated industries.

## Migration Path

GitLab provides a GitHub importer that migrates repositories, issues, PRs, wikis, and milestones. Update CI configuration from GitHub Actions to GitLab CI/CD YAML format.

## Our Take

GitLab is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your GitLab instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to GitLab?

title: GitHub vs Gitea
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs Gitea (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and Gitea are two popular version control platforms that enable developers to manage and collaborate on code repositories. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams seeking a self-hosted solution or looking to switch from a proprietary platform to an open-source alternative. The core use case for both tools is source code management, and a key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers a free plan with limited features, while Gitea is completely free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Gitea allows users to self-host their repositories, giving them full control over their data, whereas GitHub stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: GitHub has a more straightforward setup process, while Gitea requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: GitHub has better scalability and performance, thanks to its large infrastructure and resources, while Gitea's scalability depends on the user's self-hosting setup.
* Feature difference: GitHub has a more comprehensive project management feature set, including integrated issue tracking and project boards, while Gitea relies on third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Large community and ecosystem
* Integrated project management features
* Scalable and performant infrastructure
* Free plan available
* User-friendly interface
* Cons:
	+ Proprietary and closed-source
	+ Limited control over data
	+ Costs can add up for large teams
**Gitea:**
* Open-source and self-hosted
* High degree of customizability
* Low costs and no per-user fees
* Community-driven development
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve
	+ Limited project management features
	+ Requires technical expertise for self-hosting
	+ Smaller community compared to GitHub

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for large teams and enterprises that require a scalable and performant platform with integrated project management features. It's also a good choice for individuals and small teams who prioritize ease of use and don't mind the costs. On the other hand, Gitea is ideal for teams and individuals who value data ownership, customizability, and low costs. It's particularly suitable for small to medium-sized teams with technical expertise and a desire for self-hosting.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub Archive format.
2. Set up a Gitea instance on your own server or use a cloud provider.
3. Use the Gitea import tool to migrate your repository from the GitHub Archive format.
4. Configure any additional features or integrations as needed.
5. Update your team's workflows and documentation to reflect the switch to Gitea.

## Our Take
Gitea is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the polish and features of GitHub. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Gitea's search functionality is not as robust as GitHub's. However, for teams that value self-hosting and data ownership, Gitea is a viable alternative. We recommend switching to Gitea if you're a small to medium-sized team with technical expertise and a desire for customizability, but not if you rely heavily on GitHub's project management features or have a large team with complex collaboration needs.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need integrated project management features
* Technical teams who value self-hosting and data ownership
* Open-source projects with limited budgets
* Individuals who want full control over their code repositories
* Teams who prioritize customizability and low costs over ease of use

## FAQ
### Is Gitea free?
Yes, Gitea is completely free and open-source, with no costs or fees for self-hosting.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to Gitea?
Yes, you can export your GitHub repository and import it into Gitea using the Gitea import tool.
### Does Gitea have integrated project management features?
No, Gitea relies on third-party integrations for project management features, unlike GitHub which has integrated features.
### Is Gitea suitable for large teams?
Not yet, as Gitea's scalability and performance are dependent on the user's self-hosting setup, which may not be suitable for large teams.
### Can I use Gitea on a cloud provider?
Yes, you can set up a Gitea instance on a cloud provider like AWS or Google Cloud.

title: Figma vs Penpot
comparison_markdown:
# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are both design and prototyping tools used by product teams to create user interfaces and user experiences. This comparison benefits teams considering switching from Figma to Penpot, likely due to the core use case of collaborative design and the key reason of seeking a more cost-effective or open-source solution.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma charges per user, while Penpot is free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: Figma stores data on its proprietary servers, whereas Penpot allows self-hosting for full data control.
* Setup Complexity: Figma has a more streamlined setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Figma is designed for large teams and enterprises, while Penpot's scalability depends on the self-hosting infrastructure.
* Feature Difference: Figma has a more extensive library of plugins and integrations, including direct integration with popular project management tools, whereas Penpot has a growing but still limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Extensive plugin and integration library
* Streamlined setup and onboarding process
* Scalable for large teams and enterprises
* Robust customer support
* Cross-platform compatibility
### Penpot
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Growing community and open-source contributions
* Cross-platform compatibility
* Limited scalability without proper infrastructure

## When to Choose Each
Figma is the better choice for large teams and enterprises that require a robust, scalable design solution with a wide range of integrations and plugins. It's ideal for teams that prioritize ease of use and are willing to pay for the convenience and support that comes with it. 
Penpot, on the other hand, is suitable for smaller teams, startups, or individuals who are looking for a cost-effective, open-source design solution and are comfortable with the technical requirements of self-hosting. It's also a good option for teams that prioritize data ownership and control.

## Migration Path
1. Export Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to migrate designs, or manually recreate them.
3. Set up a self-hosted Penpot server or use the cloud-hosted option.
4. Configure user accounts and permissions.
5. Test and refine the migrated designs.

## Our Take
Penpot is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of Figma. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's performance can be affected by the infrastructure used for self-hosting, which may require additional technical expertise to optimize. 
However, for teams that prioritize cost-effectiveness, data ownership, and open-source principles, Penpot is a viable alternative. 
We recommend switching to Penpot for teams that are comfortable with its technical requirements and limitations, and who do not require the full range of features and integrations offered by Figma.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need advanced integrations
* Startups looking for a cost-effective design solution
* Individuals who prioritize data ownership and control
* Teams that require self-hosting for security or compliance reasons
* Designers who are comfortable with the technical requirements of Penpot

## FAQ
### Is Penpot completely free?
Yes, Penpot is free and open-source, with no costs per user. However, self-hosting may incur server costs.
### Can I migrate my Figma designs to Penpot?
Yes, you can export Figma designs in SVG or PNG format and import them into Penpot.
### Is Penpot suitable for large teams?
Not yet, as Penpot's scalability and performance may be affected by the self-hosting infrastructure.
### Does Penpot have the same features as Figma?
No, Penpot still lacks some of the features and integrations offered by Figma.
### Can I use Penpot for collaborative design?
Yes, Penpot supports real-time collaboration and commenting.
